# How do measured forces and torques, and IMU data, typically participate in stabilization when the position-controlled humanoid robot is not directly closed-loop on the real joint states within TSID?

> **Current answer:** The practitioner in the thread explains that humanoid robots with lower-level position control, such as iCub and Talos, typically use theoretical/virtual state information (TSID) in the model for open-loop calculation. The stabilizer (stabilizer) is then constructed using foot force/torque sensors and/or IMU, and the stabilizer modifies the TSID reference, for example, adjusting the center of mass (CoM) reference. He also mentions that an attempt was made to use a closed-loop floating base and maintain theoretical state information in the joints, but the complete conditions and results were not provided in the comments, so this part cannot be considered a definitive solution.

## Problem and symptoms

- Can a position-controlled robot directly compute the TSID QP using real joint/float base states, and integrate virtual states to obtain position commands?
- How can real-time deviation enter the control loop if the real state is not directly fed into the TSID?
- The system can run when only integrating virtual/command states; after calculating task error and QP with real-world state, the system diverges quickly.
- Direct feedback from real-world floating base ground truth or estimator state still causes instability.
- There is significant tracking error at the groin and ankle joints during the weight shift phase.

## Environment

- TSID; Gazebo and PyBullet; position control robot; practitioners mention iCub/Talos, and the user ultimately validated on a real machine without specifying the model.

## Priority diagnostics

- Distinguishes between the QP state used, integration start point, and feedback position of the lower-level position PID. Checks if a_sol corresponds to q_real but is derived from q_tsid integration.
- Confirm if joint feedback is handled by the lower-level position servo loop; separate the floating base/contact stability issue from the joint position loop.

## Possible causes

- The system simultaneously enters the TSID and lower-level position controller in real-world conditions.
- The acceleration derived from real-world state is used in a different virtual state integral, leading to inconsistency.

## Attempts

- The maintainer provides an open-loop TSID and control boundaries for QP. The practitioner shares the model state TSID with foot force/torque (F/T)/IMU stabilizer. The questioner attempts a real floating base, Cartesian end-effector error integration, contact reference, and gain adjustment.

## Effective fixes

- A general and clean internal thread solution is to use joint torque control; position control robots typically run the TSID with virtual model states, and the CoM is modified by F/T or IMU stabilizers.
- The user's specific machine solution does not use real floating base states, and the end-effector pose is recalibrated based on actual joint measurements, with a small bias added to the hip and ankle joints after QP.

## Result

- The reported solution works in simulation and real machine; no stability margin, parameter range, or cross-robot reproducibility was provided.

## Limitations

- The maintainer explicitly states that they do not know the clean, general solution of directly feeding real states into the position control TSID.
- End-effector error integral and joint offset are claimed hacks and cannot be directly used as general parameters for other robots.
- Discussions on contact reference height, landing rebound, and swing/contact gain have not formed a unified rule confirmed by maintainers.

## Applicability boundary

- Applicable to humanoid robots with lower-level position control, foot force/torque (F/T), or IMU. The stabilizer structure, reference correction, and gain adjustment must be individually designed for each robot.
